Experimental Results In a typical drying experiment using alternating conduction and convection, similar to a commercial bleached board machine, the instantaneous moisture content of the sample as a function of drying time is shown in Figure 5. The instantaneous sheet moisture contents are calculated following a similar method reported earlier [Sampath 2025, 2024 a and b]. Figure 5: Dry Basis Moisture vs Time for a 300 GSM Softwood Bleached Trial Figures 6a and 6b show the sample temperature and instantaneous drying rate as a function of drying time and sheet moisture content, respectively. The drying rate [g/m2s] is calculated based 14 DE-EE0009395 on the instantaneous change in sheet moisture content during an incremental time period per unit area of the sheet. It can be seen that the trends in temperature and drying rate coincides with the constant rate and falling rate periods and, in smaller timescales, coincides with each individual contact and non-contact cycle. A small delay can be seen in the drying rate peak in comparison with the temperature peak because the peak in drying rate is seen only when the contact cycle has ended, releasing the water vapor that can be measured by the laser. It is important to note that in alternating conduction and convection drying, as in multi-cylinder drying section, the instantaneous drying rates have peaks (higher drying rate) and valleys (low drying rates). The peaks in drying rate correspond to sudden increase in drying rate when the water evaporates from the heated paper and releases a burst of water vapor as it exits the cylinder (in this case the heated platen). The valleys correspond to lower drying rates at the end of the convection period during which the sheet undergoes evaporative cooling. Once it is in contact with the cylinder again both the sheet temperature and drying rate begins to increase. The sheet temperature shows a corresponding peak and valley as well. Another observation in the drying rates and sample temperatures is the higher magnitude for chamber 1 contact cycles in comparison to chamber 3 contact cycles. This behavior could be due to multiple factors including differences in the hot plate flux, dilution, and mixing of the moisture as it passes through multiple chambers to reach the laser’s detection zone (this can be seen with a wider peak for chamber 3 cycles and a taller- thinner peak for chamber 1 cycles) (Figures 6a and 6b). Figure 6a: Drying Rate and Sample Temperature vs Time for a 300 GSM Softwood Bleached Trial 15 DE-EE0009395 The average drying rate behavior with respect to moisture content shown observed here is comparable to what is reported in the literature based on intermittent gravimetric measurements (Lang, 2002, Cameron et al. 2000).
